sections.title: Asset Management
sections.content:
ASSET TRACKING BASICS
Asset management — identifying, classifying, and inventorying an organization's IT assets (hardware, software, data, personnel). Supports patching, incident response, and monitoring for unauthorized activity.
• Asset ownership assignment — designating individuals/teams responsible for specific assets (chain of accountability)
• Asset classification — organizing assets by value/sensitivity/criticality, drives consistent control application and budget priority
• Typical inventory data: type, model, serial number, asset ID, location, user(s), value, service info
ASSET ENUMERATION METHODS
Method | Description
Manual Inventory | Physical inspection, best for small orgs/specific asset types
Network Scanning | Nmap, Nessus, OpenVAS — auto-discover networked devices, open ports, services
Asset Management Software | Lansweeper, ManageEngine, SolarWinds — centralized dashboard, tracking, reporting
CMDB (Configuration Management Database) | Centralized repo of IT infrastructure/configs/relationships (ServiceNow, BMC Remedy)
MDM Solutions | Microsoft Intune, VMware Workspace ONE, MobileIron — enumerate/manage mobile assets
Cloud Asset Discovery | AWS Config, Azure Resource Graph, CloudAware, CloudCheckr
ASSET ACQUISITION/PROCUREMENT
• Prioritize vendors/products with strong built-in security (encryption, secure boot, patch support)
• Consider integration with existing security infrastructure (firewalls, IDS, SIEM)
• Assess Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) — purchase price + maintenance + incident risk
ASSET IDENTIFICATION & NAMING
• Tangible assets: barcode label or RFID tag (chip + scanner, also aids theft prevention)
• Standard naming convention — consistent identification of type/function across CMDB/DNS; should follow host/DNS naming rules
ITIL CONFIGURATION MANAGEMENT ELEMENTS
Term | Definition
Service Assets | Things/processes/people that contribute to delivering an IT service
Configuration Item (CI) | An asset requiring specific management procedures; labeled via naming convention, tracked in CMDB
Baseline Configuration | List of required settings for an asset (server/app); security baselines = minimum protection settings
Configuration Management System (CMS) | Tools/databases used to collect, store, manage CI info (spreadsheets for small nets, dedicated apps for enterprise)
• Configuration management — ensures configurable elements haven't diverged from approved config
• Change control/change management — reduces risk that changes cause operational interruption
• Diagrams best capture complex relationships: CI business workflows, logical/physical topology, rack layouts
DATA BACKUPS
Enterprise backup critical capabilities:
• Supports virtual/physical/cloud environments
• Data deduplication and compression
• Instant recovery and replication
• Ransomware protection and encryption
• Granular restore (files/folders/apps)
• Reporting/monitoring/alerting
• Integration with virtualization/cloud/storage platforms
Data Deduplication — compression technique identifying/eliminating redundant data blocks, stores one copy + references. Can be file-level, block-level, or byte-level.
Backup Location Type | Description
On-site | Local storage (HDD/tape), rapid access/recovery
Off-site | Remote location, protects against disasters/theft/ransomware
Air-gapped | Physically disconnected from network — prevents ransomware from reaching backups
RECOVERY VALIDATION
• Full recovery test — restore entire system to separate environment, verify functionality
• Partial recovery test — restore selected files/folders/databases to validate integrity
• Backup audits — check logs, schedules, configs
• Backups can report "100% success" but still fail on actual recovery — validation catches this
• Recovery times are often longer than assumed
ADVANCED DATA PROTECTION
Snapshot Type | Captures
VM Snapshot (VMware vSphere, Hyper-V) | Memory, storage, config settings of a VM; enables rollback
Filesystem Snapshot (ZFS, Btrfs) | State of filesystem at a moment; recovers deleted/corrupted files
SAN Snapshot (NetApp, Dell EMC) | Block-level storage volume state; rapid recovery of large datasets
Microsoft calls VM snapshots checkpoints.
Replication — creates/maintains exact copies of data on different systems/locations (e.g., database mirroring: primary + secondary mirrored DB).
Journaling — records changes to data in a separate log; enables undo of incomplete transactions or replay after backup. Example: JFS, NTFS journaling.
• Remote journaling — journal maintained at a separate remote location
• SAN replication — duplicates data SAN-to-SAN; synchronous (consistent) vs asynchronous (cheaper, less strict)
• VM replication — up-to-date copy of a VM on a separate host for failover
Encrypting backups — protects against unauthorized access/theft; meets regulatory requirements for sensitive data in backup sets.
SECURE DATA DESTRUCTION & ASSET DISPOSAL
Reasons for data destruction: end of retention period, legal/regulatory compliance (GDPR, HIPAA), decommissioning storage devices.
Concept | Definition
Sanitization | Removing sensitive info from media via wiping, degaussing, or encryption so it becomes irretrievable
Destruction | Physical (shredding, crushing, incinerating) or electronic (overwriting, degaussing) elimination of data
Certification | Documentation/verification of sanitization or destruction, ideally via impartial third party
Overwriting (HDD sanitization):
• Deleted files: sectors marked available, data remains until overwritten
• Zero filling — sets each bit to zero (single pass can leave recoverable patterns)
• More secure: pass of zeros, pass of ones, pass of pseudorandom pattern (some federal agencies require more than 3 passes)

sections.title: Redundancy Strategies
sections.content:
CONTINUITY OF OPERATIONS (COOP)
COOP — ensuring an organization can maintain/quickly resume critical functions during a disruption. Key elements: identify critical functions, establish priorities, determine needed resources.
• Strategies: off-site backups, failover systems, disaster recovery solutions, remote work/co-location arrangements
• Testing: tabletop exercises, isolated functional tests, full-scale drills
COOP VS. BUSINESS CONTINUITY (BC)
Concept | Scope
COOP | Immediate response/restoration of critical functions; shorter time frame
Business Continuity (BC) | Broader — overall resilience/recovery of entire org (supply chain, employee safety, legal compliance, reputation)
COOP is a component of the broader BC concept.
CAPACITY PLANNING
Assessing current/future resource needs (people, technology, infrastructure) to meet business objectives. Methods: trend analysis, simulation modeling, benchmarking.
People risk mitigations:
Strategy | Purpose
Cross-Training | Reduces dependency on single individuals/teams
Remote Work Plans | Defines comms/tech/expectations for remote operations
Alternative Reporting Structures | Backup/temporary reporting relationships, reduces single point of failure in decision-making
Remote work tech: VPN, remote desktop software, cloud-based tools (M365, Google Workspace), video conferencing, IM/chat, virtual phone systems, project management tools.
Layoff risks: disgruntled employees (unauthorized access/misuse), lost institutional knowledge, improper access revocation, theft/sabotage.
Poor capacity planning risks:
• Under-provisioning: crashes, DoS susceptibility, neglected security updates, insufficient physical security investment, overheating/power failure
• Over-provisioning: wasted cost, low utilization/poor ROI, increased complexity, opportunity cost
HIGH AVAILABILITY (HA)
Ensures systems stay operational/accessible with minimal downtime via redundant hardware, clustering, redundant networking, redundant datacenter power/cooling.
"Nines" availability table:
Nines | Availability | Annual Downtime
Six | 99.9999% | 00:00:32
Five | 99.999% | 00:05:15
Four | 99.99% | 00:52:34
Three | 99.9% | 08:45:36
Two | 99% | 87:36:00
MTD (Maximum Tolerable Downtime) — expresses availability requirement for a business function.
SCALABILITY, ELASTICITY, FAULT TOLERANCE
Term | Definition
Scalability | Capacity to increase resources to meet demand within similar cost ratios
Scale Out | Add more resources in parallel
Scale Up | Increase power of existing resources
Elasticity | System's ability to handle demand changes on demand, in real time
Fault Tolerance | System continues providing (nearly) same service level despite failures
Redundant Component | Non-essential to normal function, but enables recovery from another component's failure
SITE RESILIENCY
Site Type | Description
Hot Site | Failover almost immediately; org-owned, operational equipment, live data set
Warm Site | Similar to hot, but latest data set must be loaded
Cold Site | Longer setup; may be empty building with lease agreement
• Failover — technique ensuring a redundant component/device/site quickly takes over from a failed asset (e.g., load balancers redirecting traffic)
• Geographic dispersion — spreading recovery sites across locations to limit regional-disaster impact
Cloud as DR — cost efficiency (economies of scale), scalability without over-provisioning, geographic diversity, faster deployment, simplified management, improved security/compliance.
TESTING HA/REDUNDANCY
Test Type | Purpose
Load Testing | Validates performance under expected/peak loads
Failover Testing | Validates seamless primary→secondary transition
Testing Monitoring Systems | Validates detection/response to failures
CLUSTERING
Clustering (redundant nodes sharing data, appear as one server to clients) vs. Load Balancing (distributes traffic across independent nodes, manages web traffic).
• Virtual IP (shared/floating address) — public IP shared between clustered appliances; redundancy protocol (e.g., CARP) manages active node ownership + heartbeat for failover
Clustering Mode | Trade-off
Active/Passive (A/P) | No performance hit during failover; higher cost from unused capacity
Active/Active (A/A) | Uses full hardware capacity; performance degrades on failover as load shifts
• N+1 / N+M configurations — fewer passive nodes than active, reduces cost
• Application clustering — servers share session state so users can continue on another instance after a fault
POWER REDUNDANCY
Component | Role
Dual PSUs | Redundant power supply units; hot plug PSU replaceable without powering down
Managed PDU | Cleans power signal, protects against spikes/surges, remote monitoring/switching
UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) | Bank of batteries + inverter; bridges gap until generator/proper shutdown
Generator | Powers whole building for days; diesel/propane/natural gas or renewables (solar, wind, geothermal, hydrogen, hydro)
A UPS is always required — a generator cannot come online fast enough to prevent an interruption on its own. Generator power introduced via transfer switches (manual or automatic).
DIVERSITY AND DEFENSE IN DEPTH
• Platform diversity — using multiple OSes/technologies so a single vulnerability doesn't compromise everything
• Defense in depth — multiple layers of protection (perimeter firewalls/IDS, network segmentation, endpoint security, patch management, MFA, awareness training, incident response)
• Vendor diversity — reduces single point of failure risk; benefits: cybersecurity, business resilience, innovation, competition, customization/flexibility, risk management, compliance
• Multi-cloud strategy — diversifies risk across providers, promotes vendor independence, optimizes workload placement (e.g., primary app on one cloud, DR/backup on another)
DECEPTION & DISRUPTION TECHNOLOGIES
Tool | Purpose
Honeypot | Decoy system mimicking real systems/apps
Honeynet | Network of interconnected honeypots simulating a whole network
Honeyfile | Fake file appearing to hold sensitive info, detects access attempts
Honeytoken | False credentials/data used to distract attackers and trigger alerts
Disruption strategies: bogus DNS entries, decoy directories/dynamic pages to slow scanning, port triggering/spoofing to return fake telemetry, DNS sinkhole routing suspect traffic to a honeynet.
TESTING RESILIENCY
Test Type | Description
Tabletop Exercises | Teams discuss/work through hypothetical scenarios
Failover Tests | Intentional failure of primary to verify automatic transfer
Simulations | Controlled experiments replicating real-world scenarios
Parallel Processing Tests | Run primary + backup simultaneously to validate backup capacity
Documentation: test plans (objectives/scope/methods/roles), test scripts (step-by-step), test results (strengths/weaknesses). Third-party assessments/certifications (ISO 22301, PCI DSS, SOC 2) offer objective evaluation.

sections.title: Physical Security
sections.content:
PHYSICAL ACCESS CONTROL FUNDAMENTALS
Same AAA fundamentals as technical security:
• Authentication — access lists, mechanisms to allow approved persons through barriers
• Authorization — barriers around a resource, controlled entry/exit points
• Accounting — records entry/exit use, detects breaches
Physical security is implemented in zones — each separated by barriers, progression should be increasingly restrictive.
SITE LAYOUT, FENCING, LIGHTING
Control | Notes
Barricades | Channel people through defined entry/exit points; not fully effective alone
Bollards | Short posts (steel/concrete); block vehicle access, protect pedestrians; can be fixed/retractable
Fencing | Should be transparent, robust, climb-resistant (height + razor wire); intimidating appearance trade-off
Lighting | Deters intrusion, aids surveillance/facial recognition; must avoid shadow/glare
Existing structure design principles:
• Locate secure zones deep within building, away from external walls/doors/windows
• Use DMZ-style layout — public areas away from secure zones
• Visible signage/warnings for deterrence; discreet entry points to secure zones
• Minimize cross-zone traffic; use one-way glass in secure zones
GATEWAYS AND LOCKS
Lock Type | Description
Physical | Conventional key locks; resistance to picking varies by cost
Electronic | PIN/cipher/combination/keyless; smart lock via magnetic swipe or proximity reader
Biometric | Integrated with a biometric scanner
• Access control vestibule (mantrap) — two interlocking doors, only one door opens at a time, prevents tailgating; used in datacenters/gov buildings/financial institutions
• Cable locks — secure device chassis to rack/desk (e.g., Kensington slot), prevent case opening
ACCESS BADGES & PACS
Access badges — magnetic strip/RFID/NFC cards replacing physical keys; requires magnetic locks + card readers (needs power + network).
Physical Access Control System (PACS) — hardware + software (badges, readers, control panels, centralized network) managing facility access; logs badge activity (time, location, identity) for audits/investigations/evacuation planning.
SECURITY GUARDS AND CAMERAS
Method | Trade-off
Security Guards | Effective deterrent, intuition-based response; expensive; can't access all security-clearance zones
Video Surveillance (CCTV) | Cheaper than guards; records movement; slower response time, needs sufficient monitoring staff
AI/ML camera capabilities:
• Motion Recognition — gait identification, alerts on unrecognized movement patterns
• Object Detection — flags environmental changes (missing server, unknown device)
• Drones/UAV — cover wider areas than ground patrols
ALARM SYSTEMS
Alarm Type | Trigger
Circuit | Circuit opened/closed (door/window/fence); closed-circuit more secure than open-circuit
Motion Detection | Microwave radio reflection or passive infrared (PIR)
Noise Detection | Microphone-triggered; AI reduces false positives
Proximity | RFID tags/readers track tagged object movement
Duress | Manually triggered by staff under threat (pendant, hidden trigger, duress PIN)
A silent alarm alerts security personnel rather than sounding audibly.
SENSOR TYPES
Sensor | Detection Method | Common Use
Infrared | Heat pattern changes | Motion detection systems
Pressure | Weight activation | Floor/mat sensors, high-security or retail foot traffic
Microwave | Reflection off moving objects | Combined with IR (dual-tech), reduces false alarms; outdoor areas
Ultrasonic | Sound wave return time | Automated lighting systems

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
• Perform asset identification and catalog all physical/intangible assets (type, location, value, ownership)
• Implement asset lifecycle management (procurement, maintenance, depreciation, retirement)
• Perform asset tracking, especially for mobile/theft-prone assets
• Understand regulatory compliance requirements for specific asset categories
• Perform disaster recovery/business continuity planning to restore critical assets
• Use legally compliant, secure asset disposal (data destruction) methods
• Ensure adequate capacity planning for people, technology, and infrastructure
• Implement high availability strategies: scalability/elasticity, fault tolerance/redundancy, clustering, site resiliency
• Use risk assessments to identify high-availability-requirement assets and provision redundancy:
• Hot/warm/cold site resources for disaster recovery
• Dual power supply, PDUs, PSUs, and generators for power resilience
• NIC teaming, multiple paths, and load balancing for network resilience
• RAID and multipath I/O for storage resilience
• Implement diversity in technologies and controls
• Perform comprehensive testing of resiliency capabilities
• Design sites as zones for maximum access control/surveillance; use industrial camouflage, perimeter networks, air gaps, vaults/safes where applicable
• Secure the site perimeter with fencing, barricades/bollards, and locks (physical, electronic, biometric); use clone/skim-resistant smart cards
• Monitor with security guards, CCTV, and drones/UAV; use effective lighting to maximize surveillance
• Deploy alarm systems (circuit, motion, proximity, duress) to detect intrusion
• Use ID badges to authorize access

concept_cards.hook: Security copy of production data made to removable media on a schedule (full, incremental, differential).
Standby power supply (diesel/propane) providing power after a UPS bridges the initial gap.
Load balancing technique where servers work together as a unit.
Identifies how business processes handle minor/disaster-level disruption via processing redundancy.
Policies and processes that ensure asset and service purchases/contracts are fully managed, secure, use authorized suppliers/vendors, and meet business goals.
Third-party asset disposal technique using sanitization/destruction, with documentary evidence.
Asset disposal ensuring physically inaccessible/irrevocable data remnants (degaussing, shredding, incineration).
Policies governing device/software removal from production and subsequent disposal.

practice_questions.q: A web application runs on two servers; if one fails, the other takes over automatically. What is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Failover keeps a service running when a component fails.

practice_questions.q: A company keeps a list of every laptop, its owner, location and serial number. What process is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Inventory tracks what the organization owns.

practice_questions.q: An attacker modifies the amount on a wire transfer while it is in transit. Which part of the CIA triad was violated?
practice_questions.explanation: Unauthorized modification of data is an integrity failure.

practice_questions.q: A backup site with power and network but no installed equipment, which takes weeks to bring online, is a:
practice_questions.explanation: Cold sites are cheap but slow to activate.

practice_questions.q: Before a hard drive is reused by another department, data must be removed so it cannot be recovered. What is this called?
practice_questions.explanation: Sanitization makes data unrecoverable before reuse.

practice_questions.q: A sender digitally signs a contract so they cannot later deny having sent it. Which concept does this provide?
practice_questions.explanation: A digital signature ties the message to the signer's private key, preventing denial.

practice_questions.q: A fully equipped site with live data replication that can take over within minutes is a:
practice_questions.explanation: Hot sites are ready almost immediately but are expensive.

practice_questions.q: Drives are shredded and a vendor provides a document proving it. What is that document called?
In the AAA framework, which step decides what a user is allowed to do after they log in?
practice_questions.explanation: Authorization grants permissions after identity is proven.

practice_questions.q: What does recovery time objective (RTO) measure?
options: The maximum acceptable time to restore a service
The time to detect an incident
practice_questions.explanation: RTO is how long the business can tolerate downtime.
